title: Dry-run: controlling a CDN from the origin

spec.title: Dry-run: controlling a CDN from the origin
spec.intro: About 4 minutes. The CDN's edge network is infra you don't write — the code you do write is the handful of headers that tell it what to do.

steps.title: Cache-Control is the entire contract with the edge
steps.explain: The origin doesn't push content to edge nodes — it answers requests as they arrive at the edge, and the response headers are the only instruction the CDN gets about how long to keep what it just fetched.
steps.saysOutLoud: The CDN doesn't know your data's lifecycle — the header is the only thing telling it.

steps.title: The edge network itself is infrastructure, not app code
steps.explain: Hundreds of geographically distributed PoPs, each with its own cache and routing to the nearest one via anycast, are entirely the CDN provider's infrastructure. The app team never provisions a PoP — the leverage is purely in what headers the origin sends and what the CDN config allows.

steps.title: First request at a PoP is a real trip to the origin
steps.explain: A cache miss at the edge triggers a synchronous fetch back to the origin before the edge can respond — the very first user hitting a new PoP pays full origin latency, everyone after them at that PoP gets the cached copy until it expires.

steps.title: Stale content needs an explicit purge, not a shorter TTL
steps.explain: Waiting out the TTL is fine for routine changes but too slow when content was wrong and needs to disappear now — a purge API call tells every PoP holding that URL to drop it immediately, independent of whatever max-age was set.

steps.title: A cache key that ignores query params serves the wrong content
steps.explain: If the CDN's cache key is just the path, `/image.jpg?w=200` and `/image.jpg?w=800` collide — whichever request hits a given PoP first gets cached and served to everyone else at that size, silently, until it expires.

steps.title: Stampede protection at the origin, not just the edge
steps.explain: When an object expires simultaneously across many PoPs — a popular asset with a short TTL — they can all miss at once and hit the origin together. Origin-side request coalescing collapses those into one real fetch, the same single-flight pattern used for any cache stampede.

spec.closing: If they ask push vs pull: pull-through (what's shown here) only ever fetches what was actually requested, so it's simpler and the default choice — push CDNs, where the origin proactively uploads content, only earn their complexity when you can predict demand ahead of the request, like a scheduled livestream.
